_comment: Rules the core itself declares for mechanism-guard (CONVENTIONS: a tool ships mechanism-rules.json at its root; the guard reads it from the enabled plugin). Each rule names the defined path in `instead`.

rules.was: a PR merge through the raw API (gh api -X PUT .../pulls/<n>/merge) - the usual way to re-issue a merge the permission layer refused for `gh pr merge`
rules.instead: A refused action is not re-issued in another form (rules/working-rules.md, Mechanism Discipline, 'A refusal is a decision'). Report what was refused and for what; the merge goes through `gh pr merge` once permitted, or through the party/operator who holds the right.

rules.was: waiting for CI in the foreground - a core CI run takes about 15 minutes and holds the whole session; several PRs in a row cost hours
rules.instead: Start the same command with Bash run_in_background and keep working; the verdict arrives as a notification (Working Rule #9). Not through Monitor: the harness ends a Monitor after 30 min at most, and a core CI run takes about 36 min (2026-10-26). Several PRs: one detached watch each, in parallel.

rules.was: running the local CI mirror in the foreground - measured 2026-10-25 on the macOS instance: the lint job runs the fixture suites and holds the session for minutes, the operator had to background it by hand
rules.instead: Start the same command detached (Bash run_in_background, or Monitor) and keep working; read its summary line before claiming green (Working Rule #13).

rules.was: multi-line text written into the command itself (a `git commit -m` message, a `gh pr|issue` body or title spanning lines) - permission rules match the whole command text with wildcards, so a word in the text trips an ask rule: measured 2026-10-26 on the Windows instance, a commit message naming `git -C <brain> push` and `main-push` matched the template's `git -C * push * main*` ask and prompted the operator in the middle of an autonomous run
rules.instead: Write the text to a file in the scratchpad and pass the file: `git commit -F <file>`, `gh pr create|comment --body-file <file>` (Working Rule #8: multi-line content goes into a file). A one-line `-m` stays fine.

rules.was: a self-written wait loop (until/while ... sleep N) in the foreground - measured 2026-10-26 on the macOS instance: a loop waiting for two test runs held the session until the operator pressed ctrl+b; the two rules above list commands by NAME, the loop is the generic form of the same wait
rules.instead: Start the loop detached (Bash run_in_background, or Monitor) and keep working; its end arrives as a notification. A background job you already started notifies on its own - no loop needed (Working Rule #13).

rules.was: a waiting script (wait-*.sh, *-watch.sh: reconnect, link, collab, repo-activity, shared-memory watches) in the foreground - the class sweep of the wait-loop rule (2026-10-26): these scripts are the same wait under a name, and only ci-watch.sh was listed
rules.instead: Start it detached (Monitor for a stream of events, Bash run_in_background for one verdict) and keep working (Working Rule #13). A help call passes, and so do the `status`/`disarm` subcommands of the two scripts that have them (repo-activity-watch.sh, shared-memory-watch.sh) - collab-watch.sh has none: `collab-watch.sh status` ARMS the watch (measured 2026-10-26).

rules.was: a destructive push in a form no permission pattern can catch: a branch delete by colon refspec (`git push origin :feat`), or a force/mirror push behind `git -c k=v` - a deny pattern ending in `:*` is read as a trailing wildcard (docs permissions: `Bash(ls:*)` equals `Bash(ls *)`), so `git push * :*` would deny every push with two arguments, and `-c` moves `push` out of every prefix pattern (found 2026-10-26 by the macOS instance's review of the settings template); since 2026-11-02 every `git [-C <repo>] push` form, plus --delete/-d and --no-verify (skips the pre-push hook): the settings template dropped its `git -C * push …` text rules because they matched commit messages too
rules.instead: Deleting a remote branch or rewriting remote history is the operator's word (destructive). A merged PR's branch goes with `gh pr merge --delete-branch`; anything else: report it and wait for the word.

rules.was: a push past the core's pre-push hook with its marker PUSH_GUARD_OK (a delete, a rewrite, or main of a repo not in .claude/rules/push-targets.json) - the hook replaced the permission dialog, so its marker carries the operator's word like the dialog did (2026-11-02)
rules.instead: Main of a repo outside the list goes through a PR; a rewrite or delete is the operator's word. With that word: PUSH_GUARD_OK="<reason>" git -C <repo> push ... # MECHANISM-OK: "<operator words>" YYYY-MM-DD

rules.was: a Monitor stream piped through `grep` without `--line-buffered` - the filter holds its matches in a buffer, the events arrive late or never, and the watch looks dead (measured 2026-10-11 on the macOS instance: a measurement watcher wrote only at its end, the operator saw 'nothing happens')
rules.instead: Give every grep in the stream `--line-buffered` (awk: `fflush()`); then the first match reaches the session as it happens. A one-shot `grep -q` after the stream ended is no stream and does not need it.

rules.was: moving a marketplace pin (any write to a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`: editor script, sed -i, cp, redirect) - a pin pulls a plugin update onto EVERY consumer of the marketplace, other parties included; ported 2026-10-28 from an instance rule that only one brain carried. Read-only access (cat, head, grep, jq, sed -n, awk, diff, cmp, git diff/log/show, `gh api` without a method or field flag - a GET of the remote file) passes
rules.instead: A pin moves on its owner's word: the core channel on the operator's word, a suite's pin on the word of that suite's owner (the owner's own pin PR is that word). A green CI run, a measurement on both systems or a hold field that reads its own condition as met is no substitute - those are artefacts the AI wrote. After every move run the marketplace's own pin check and read its verdict.

rules.was: waiting for CI through a hand-built poll loop (while/until/sleep around gh pr checks / gh run) - also when detached: `gh pr checks` exits 8 while checks run, an ad-hoc loop reads that as an error and swallows it, and silence looks like 'still running' (measured: 60 historical cases on the macOS instance; the Windows instance's #109 incident)
rules.instead: core/scripts/ci-watch.sh pr <owner/repo> <nr> (or ref <owner/repo> <ref>), started detached (Bash run_in_background). Exit 0 green, 1 red, 2 NOT measurable (loud, not green), 3 the repo has no CI. A compound that calls ci-watch.sh itself passes.

rules.was: a waiting script armed with '&' or with its output thrown away - the process hangs on the tool session and dies with it, the harness never knows it and can never notify; measured 2026-08-08 on the macOS instance: an operator's restart ran into nothing
rules.instead: Start it with Bash run_in_background (or Monitor for a stream), never with '&'. Its OUTPUT is the report path: no >/dev/null. Afterwards check that it runs.

rules.was: a CI or check status cut down by tail/head - a part is read as the whole; measured 2026-08-10 on the macOS instance: `gh pr checks --watch | tail -3` showed the last (green) lines, the red run above was cut off
rules.instead: Read the verdict from the machine state, never from a filtered subset: the exit code of `gh pr checks`, or `--json conclusion` per run; look at the full output or the exit code.

rules.was: a shell heredoc (<<MARKER) - Working Rule #8 (multi-line content goes into a file): it trips the obfuscation heuristics and bypasses the file tools; measured 2026-08-13 on the macOS instance: four heredocs in one day despite the rule and two announcements to stop
rules.instead: Write the content to a file in the scratchpad (the Write tool), then run or append it: a script = Write <scratchpad>/x.py + python3 <scratchpad>/x.py; an append = Edit/Write on the target file. A one-line `python3 -c '...'` is fine. A here-string (<<<) is no heredoc.

rules.was: a push into another repo through a cd chain (cd <path> && git push) - Working Rule #8: another directory goes through the tool's own flag; the cd chain matches no permission pattern and walks past the list
rules.instead: git -C <abs-path> push (the form permission patterns are written for); inside the repo itself a plain `git push`.

rules.was: CI runs read without a workflow filter (`gh run list` without --workflow/-w) - a repo has several workflows (CI, a text-leak check on every comment, CodeQL); the newest N runs mix them and push the CI runs out. Measured 2026-10-28 on the macOS instance: four green runs of the comment-triggered workflow were taken for CI runs on the same commit and a red main was called green, twice in one evening; a readiness reader with the same query reported no red CI while two CI runs on main were red. ci-watch.sh had learned this earlier, the lesson stayed in that one tool
rules.instead: For a verdict on a commit: `scripts/ci-watch.sh` (reads `actions/runs?head_sha=`, detached as Working Rule #9 says). To look: `gh run list --workflow <name> ...` with the workflow you mean (e.g. `--workflow CI`).

rules.was: a second output-style source under .claude/output-styles/ - the core ships its style through the plugin (output-styles/, force-for-plugin: true); a brain's own copy is a second source that drifts from the core's text (measured on the Windows instance: the instance carried this rule since 2026-08-04, after a copied style had diverged)
rules.instead: The style comes from the enabled core plugin. If it does not take effect: update the marketplace and the plugin (`bash core/scripts/brain-update.sh`), then start a new session - do not copy the file. A brain that really wants its own style names it in .claude/rules/local-machinery.json.

rules.was: a second output-style source under .claude/output-styles/ (written through Write/Edit)
rules.instead: The style comes from the enabled core plugin. If it does not take effect: update the marketplace and the plugin (`bash core/scripts/brain-update.sh`), then start a new session - do not copy the file. A brain that really wants its own style names it in .claude/rules/local-machinery.json.

rules.was: an inline script in double quotes (`python3 -c "..."`, `node -e "..."`, `bash -c "..."`) whose text holds a backtick or `$(` - the shell runs that part as a command before the interpreter sees the text. Measured 2026-11-03 on the Windows instance: two backtick paths in a protocol entry ran as shell scripts (no file changed, the written text lost both paths); replay over that brain's transcripts: 4 such calls in 2 sessions. The macOS instance carried the same rule as instance data since 2026-10-29 (a PR text lost three names).
rules.instead: Multi-line or quoted text goes into a file (Working Rule #8): write the script with the Write tool and run the file, or quote the argument in single quotes. An escaped backtick (\`) is no hit.

rules.was: a path list passed to git as an unquoted shell variable (`git add $F`): zsh does not split it into words, so it arrives as ONE path with spaces; bash splits it, PowerShell does neither - the same command means three things. Measured 2026-11-02 on the macOS instance, twice in one project ("pathspec ... did not match any files").
rules.instead: Write the paths out (one call, by path - Working Rule #12). In a script of your own use an array ("${ARR[@]}" in bash, ${=VAR} only in zsh).

rules.was: git stash - also in a worktree of your own: the stash lives in the repository that every worktree of it shares, so it is visible and poppable from each of them. Measured 2026-11-02 on the macOS instance: a stash for a negative control emptied the worktree's changes, and the control ran against the wrong test. shared-working-copy-guard covers stash only while a second session shares the same checkout.
rules.instead: Run a negative control against the old state in a folder of its own: `git show origin/main:<path> > <scratch>/negctl/<file>` and the test there. Commit your own paths instead of stashing (Working Rule #12). `git stash list` / `git stash show` only read and pass.

rules.was: an office file (Word, Excel, PowerPoint) built by a generic converter (textutil, pandoc, soffice --convert-to). Measured 2026-11-11 on the macOS instance: textutil turned 10.5 pt into 12 pt and wrote no page size or margins, so a page that fit in the preview ran over in Word.
rules.instead: Build office files through the office skill of the harness (docx, xlsx, pptx — page size, margins and sizes set explicitly). Reading an office file into text or Markdown (`-convert txt`, `pandoc a.docx -o a.md`) stays free.

rules.was: a shop SEARCH page opened as a tab for the operator (measured 2026-11-11 on the macOS instance: 81 order tabs, most of them search pages, because the order list carried article numbers). A search result is no order position.
rules.instead: Order tabs only through `python3 core/scripts/product-sources.py open <order-list.csv>` - every line a product page with an availability read under 24 h. When no product page is found, say which shop does not carry it and name the link, never open it.

rules.was: browser tabs opened by an AppleScript of its own, past the order-list check (same incident: the tabs were opened from a URL file via osascript, which the open-command rule did not see).
rules.instead: `python3 core/scripts/product-sources.py open <order-list.csv>` opens the tabs after the check. Reading the browser (`osascript -e 'tell application "Safari" to get URL of ...'`) stays free.

rules.was: a core gate or check run through a pipe (`leak-scan.py | tail`) - the pipeline's exit code is the LAST command's, so a red gate reads green. Measured 2026-08-04 on the Windows instance: a red gate slipped through into a commit and a push; ported 2026-11-07 from that instance's rule data (in use since 2026-08-04, command position anchored 2026-08-08 so reading a script with `git show ... | sed` passes)
rules.instead: Run the gate without a pipe and read its exit code on its own (`python3 core/scripts/leak-scan.py; echo "exit=$?"`), or write the output to a file first and filter that.

rules.was: `claude plugin update` without a marketplace refresh before it - a stale marketplace clone pins an older version and writes the fix back. Measured 2026-08-04 on the Windows instance; ported 2026-11-07 from that instance's rule data. A refresh earlier in the same command passes; the command position is anchored, so the phrase quoted in a message is no hit
rules.instead: Core update: `bash core/scripts/brain-update.sh` (follows the pin of the enabled channel). A single suite plugin: `claude plugin marketplace update <marketplace>` first, then `claude plugin update <plugin>@<marketplace>`. If the refresh already ran in this session, repeat the command with `# MECHANISM-OK: marketplace refresh ran in this session`.
